extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and developers interested in Twine and interactive fiction (game writers, digital storytelling scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: A research-guide page that defines interactive fiction subtypes (parser- vs choice-based), describes visual novels and kinetic novels, and lists development tools and community resources useful for creating or researching interactive, nonlinear text games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive fiction — genre definition and two-category classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive fiction is a genre of games where players move through the story of a game told primarily through text, either by typing in text commands or clicking a line of text written as a series of choices. Interactive fiction games generally fall into two categories, named after how they function: 'parser-based' games (for text commands typed on a keyboard) and 'choice-based' games (for text-based choices shown and picked on a screen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to determine the interaction model for a project (typed-parser input vs. choice/selection). The guide's paraphrase of IFWiki establishes these two high-level design families as primary distinguishing features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parser-based interactive fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Parser-based games (for text commands typed on a keyboard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your work relies on free-form textual commands and natural-language-like input, treat it as parser-based IF; evaluate design and implementation choices against expectations for parser handling, parsing robustness, and affordances for textual input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice-based interactive fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice-based games (for text-based choices shown and picked on a screen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the narrative advances via selectable options rather than typed commands, classify it as choice-based IF; Twine games and visual novels are popular examples of this form and design decisions should prioritize branch structure, choice clarity, and UX for selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual novel characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual novels are a type of interactive fiction game 'with a large text based storyline and only little interaction of the player.' They are usually designed with animated characters in the foreground and a stylized environmental background, with dialogue written below the characters in a text box. Players of visual novels progress through the story by reading dialogue and narration, and then sometimes making choices between lines of dialogue, places, or characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating visual novels, consider the prominence of textual narrative, the role (and minimalism) of player interaction, presentation (character sprites, background art), and the UI for dialogue. The guide also notes the sub-type 'kinetic novels' where players make no choices and simply read through the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinetic novel (no-choice visual novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinetic novels are visual novels where players made no choices and instead simply progressed through the story by reading dialogue and narration with limited controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kinetic novels emphasize linear narrative delivery and should be evaluated primarily on prose, pacing, audiovisual presentation, and clarity of progression rather than branching design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool choice — Twine suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Twine: 'An open-source tool for telling interactive, nonlinear stories', created and led by Chris Klimas. Free and open source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select Twine when you need an accessible, open-source environment for creating nonlinear, choice-based text games. Use it for rapid prototyping and authoring of hypertext narratives; consult Twine-specific manuals and customization options for advanced features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool choice — ChoiceScript suitability and licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: ChoiceScript: 'A simple programming language for writing interactive novels', created by Choice of Games, and used to develop games sold under the Choice of Games brand. Free to download; commercial use requires Choice of Games company as publisher or license vendor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ChoiceScript if you want a language tailored to choice-based novels and you accept its commercial-use licensing constraints. Consider licensing requirements early if you plan to monetize or publish commercially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool choice — Ink suitability and engine integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Ink: 'A narrative scripting language for games', created by Inkle Studios, and known as the scripting language for their games, such as Heaven’s Vault. Free and open source; middleware for integration with Unity and Unreal Engine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose Ink when you need a script-language focused on narrative that can integrate with game engines (Unity/Unreal). It is suitable for projects requiring engine-level features, richer interactivity, or complex state management tied to visuals/physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool choice — Dendry (hypertext command-line tooling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dendry: A set 'of command line tools and a common file format for hypertext interactive fiction', originally created by Ian Millington and revived by Autumn Chen. Free and open source; heavily inspired by the defunct Varytale engine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider Dendry for workflows that favor command-line tooling and standardized file formats for hypertext IF; useful for developers who want scriptable build pipelines or interoperability with other hypertext tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool choice — Ren'Py for visual novels and multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Ren'Py: 'A visual novel engine that helps you use words, images, and sounds to tell interactive stories that run on computers and mobile devices.' Free and open source; incorporates Python scripting for complex development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Ren'Py for visual novels that require integrated multimedia (images, sound) and programmatic control via Python. Evaluate projects for need of animation, audio, platform deployment, and Python-level custom behavior when selecting this engine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community resources for discovery, collaboration, and promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive Fictions: 'We're a directory meant to help to build a stronger community within the interactive fiction genre.' A blog for interactive fiction game developers to share their work, compile coding resources, and spotlight diverse creators, genres, and themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage community directories, blogs, and spotlight features to find collaborators, gather tutorials, and promote games. Community resources are important for building audience and for peer learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with festivals and showcases (LudoNarraCon)
rubrics_metrics.description: LudoNarraCon: 'A digital festival celebrating narrative games' presented by Fellow Traveler... They focus on story-rich games, including interactive fiction games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit to or participate in narrative-focused festivals and showcases to get visibility, network with other creators, and situate work within contemporary narrative-game conversations.
